output.brief: The gap looks mostly like a difference in time in role, not work location. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so most remote staff are new: 32% of them had the 18 months in level the policy requires, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28% vs 29%), approval rates (71% vs 74%) and overall promotion rates (20% vs 21%) are almost the same. The expected remote rate from this mix is 8.2%, against 7.6% observed. Remote staff don't leave more often, and the job-family explanation doesn't hold. One caveat: only 110 remote staff are eligible, so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. Evidence on unequal access to high-profile work is anecdotal. Don't confirm proximity bias, and don't adopt the three-day office rule. It would penalise about 180 people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread comparison. Next: hold the proposal. Change reporting to compare eligible people only, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Meanwhile, collect staffing data on who gets stretch assignments. Clear communication of the promotion criteria to remote staff is a cheap extra step.
